problem: This preprint measures how the choice of quantum feature map changes the classification results of a quantum kernel SVM on medical data.
gap: Encoding classical data is essential, but its specific effect on classification outcomes had been little explored.
method: The authors computed kernel matrices from nine feature maps and applied them to the original Wisconsin Breast Cancer dataset and the TCGA Glioma dataset, comparing classifier performance and execution time.
results: Feature maps built on Rx gates worked best for the Wisconsin data, and Ry gates worked best for Glioma, on both performance and time. The choice of map clearly affected outcomes.
limits: It uses the original Wisconsin dataset rather than the Diagnostic version studied here, compares no wider classical model set in its abstract, and is a preprint.
mm: Wisconsin Breast Cancer (original) and TCGA Glioma
f: Rx maps best for Wisconsin; Ry maps best for Glioma

problem: This study evaluates quantum models for breast cancer diagnosis under a deliberately strict protocol, without expecting them to win.
gap: Many comparisons use one internal hold-out result and omit calibration, decision value and explainability.
method: Using WDBC for development and an independent Wisconsin cohort for external validation, it compared five classical learners, an eight-qubit VQC, a ZZ-feature-map QSVM and a hybrid ensemble.
results: Internally the RBF SVM reached AUC 0.998, while the QSVM reached only 0.727. Externally the VQC scored 0.983, with intervals overlapping the best models. Z-rotation embeddings collapsed the VQC to chance.
limits: The authors stress that curated benchmark data does not establish clinical readiness, and the classical models are already close to the performance ceiling on this dataset.
technique: VQC, ZZ QSVM and classical benchmark
mm: WDBC (n=569) and external WBC (n=683); ablation and noise tests
f: RBF SVM AUC 0.998; ZZ QSVM 0.727; external VQC 0.983
l: Benchmark data only; not clinical readiness

problem: This work investigates whether empirical quantum advantage can be found on real healthcare data.
gap: Provable advantages existed for synthetic data, but it had not been studied empirically whether advantage is attainable, or on which data.
method: The authors built an end-to-end framework over electronic health record subsets with 5 to 20 features and 200 to 300 training samples. RBF SVMs were compared with quantum kernel models run on an IBM quantum computer.
results: Regimes where quantum kernels might help were identified, and a new terrain ruggedness index was proposed for estimating how a model will perform on a dataset.
limits: The framework identifies where advantage could occur for selected subsets, not across clinical data generally. Further validation on independent cohorts is therefore still required.
mm: EHR subsets; 5-20 features; 200-300 samples; IBM hardware
f: Regimes of possible advantage found; ruggedness index proposed

problem: This paper introduces new quantum neural network methods and tests them on medical image classification.
gap: Quantum methods needed efficient training procedures and direct comparison with classical networks on real hardware.
method: The authors present an orthogonal network based on a pyramidal circuit, and quantum-assisted networks that use a quantum computer for inner product estimation. They compared quantum and classical methods on hardware and simulators.
results: Quantum and classical neural networks gave a similar level of accuracy, and the new training algorithms were proven to scale asymptotically better than earlier ones.
limits: Similar accuracy is not an advantage, and the authors tie the promise of these methods to the arrival of better quantum hardware. Practical benefit in imaging thus remains prospective.
mm: Medical image tasks on hardware and simulators
f: Quantum and classical accuracy similar; training scales better
l: No accuracy advantage; depends on better hardware

problem: This foundational paper introduces a quantum layer for extracting image features within a convolutional architecture.
gap: CNNs depend on hierarchical feature extraction, and it was unknown whether small quantum transformations could usefully contribute to this on near-term devices.
method: Quanvolutional layers transform local patches of input with random quantum circuits. Three model types were compared on MNIST: CNNs, quanvolutional networks, and CNNs with added non-linearities.
results: The quanvolutional models gave higher test accuracy and faster training than the purely classical CNNs. The small circuits need little or no error correction.
limits: MNIST is an easy benchmark and the abstract's accuracy claim is limited to those models. Whether the benefit is uniquely quantum, and whether it survives on harder images, is not settled.
f: Higher test accuracy and faster training than purely classical CNNs
l: Easy benchmark; quantum origin of benefit unsettled

problem: This study develops two hybrid quantum models for image classification that can operate within near-term limits.
gap: Circuits with many qubits are not yet feasible, so image classification needs designs built from smaller quantum parts.
method: The first model uses parallel quantum circuits and was tested on MNIST, Medical MNIST and CIFAR-10. The second uses a quanvolutional layer to reduce image resolution.
results: The first model reached 99.21% on full MNIST using one-eighth of the parameters of the matching classical model, above 99% on Medical MNIST and above 82% on CIFAR-10. The second equalled the classical version with a quarter of the parameters.
limits: The models are heavily hybrid, so results cannot be attributed to the quantum layers alone, and their performance on noisy hardware is not reported in the abstract.
f: 99.21% on MNIST with eight times fewer parameters
l: Heavily hybrid; noisy hardware not reported

problem: This paper proposes a quantum convolutional network that lowers computational complexity on NISQ devices.
gap: Near-term models must be practical in size and noise tolerance, and they need implementable circuits that correspond to specific classical kernels.
method: The design uses a number of basic gates polylogarithmic in input size. Numerical simulations cover spatial filtering, namely smoothing, sharpening and edge detection, as well as handwritten number recognition.
results: Complexity is greatly reduced compared with classical counterparts, the model tolerates certain noise in image recognition, and its parameters do not depend on input size. It maps classical filters directly to quantum circuits.
limits: Results come from numerical simulation on simple image tasks, the noise robustness applies only to certain noise, and costs of loading data are not discussed in the abstract.
mm: Simulated filtering and handwritten number recognition
f: Reduced complexity; parameters independent of input size
l: Simulation on simple tasks; only certain noise tolerated

problem: This review assesses the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and its variants for combinatorial optimisation.
gap: Researchers needed clear guidance on whether QAOA can beat classical algorithms and in which circumstances it should be used.
method: The authors overview QAOA performance across problem types and scenarios, examine hardware concerns, including how errors and noise affect it, and carry out a comparative study of selected extensions.
results: The review presents the current state of the algorithm and its variants, along with future directions and a short practical guide for applying it.
limits: The abstract treats classical competitiveness as a question to examine rather than a settled result. The review format also means that claims depend on the varied studies that it collects.
mm: Survey and comparison of QAOA variants
f: Current status of QAOA and a practical guide provided
l: Advantage over classical not settled in abstract

problem: This experiment searches for a quantum speed-up on a hard practical problem, maximum independent set.
gap: Realising a speed-up on relevant, computationally hard problems remains a central open challenge.
method: Two-dimensional arrays of Rydberg atoms, reaching 289 qubits, were programmed with an encoding based on the blockade effect, and variational algorithms were optimised in a closed loop on graphs of chosen connectivity. Results were benchmarked against simulated annealing.
results: Problem hardness was governed by solution degeneracy and the number of local minima. On the hardest graphs, the team saw a superlinear speed-up for exact solutions when circuits were deep.
limits: The comparison is with simulated annealing specifically, on one class of graphs, so it does not establish an advantage over every classical solver.
mm: Up to 289 qubits; maximum independent set; programmable graphs
f: Superlinear speed-up over simulated annealing on hardest graphs
l: One classical comparator and graph class

problem: This perspective reviews where quantum algorithms may help optimisation and how such claims should be tested.
gap: Interest in quantum optimisation is widespread, but approaches differ across fields and comparisons with classical methods need clear standards.
method: The authors use complexity theory to separate provably exact from heuristic settings, outline algorithmic building blocks and problem classes, and analyse the effects of scaling on noisy devices.
results: They identify key open questions, propose metrics for fair classical comparison, and suggest finance and sustainability as sources of benchmark problems.
limits: It sets out an agenda rather than demonstrating a new advantage, and its metrics and benchmarks must still be adopted and tested by future experimental work.
mm: Complexity analysis, building blocks, benchmarking metrics
f: Open questions and fair comparison metrics proposed
l: Agenda only; no new advantage demonstrated
